title: Good Reasons to Withhold the Truth
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece pushes back on absolutist honesty, arguing that withholding the truth is sometimes the ethical choice rather than a moral failing. It opens with an extreme example, deceiving someone to prevent violence to a third party, to establish that context matters more than a blanket rule. From there it moves to everyday cases: protecting a confidence, sparing someone needless embarrassment, or avoiding unnecessary hurt. The article is careful to distinguish self-serving deception, which it condemns, from other-protecting discretion, which it treats as compatible with being a fundamentally honest person, while still affirming that candor is the long-term foundation of trust.
points: Withholding the truth is sometimes the right thing to do, not automatically a moral failing.
The key distinction is deceiving to protect others versus deceiving to protect or benefit yourself.
Preventing harm to a third party is offered as the clearest justification for withholding truth.
Protecting a confidence or sparing someone unnecessary embarrassment are everyday examples.
Long-term relationships still depend on candor and honesty as the general rule.
quotes: Even good people withhold the truth on occasion and, in many instances, it is the right thing to do.
Those among us who believe withholding the truth is never justified haven't thought deeply about the complexity of human relationships.
Good leaders are truthful people who work hard not to distort reality.
Deceiving others to prevent violence or abuse is still deception. Yet, it is the right thing to do.
When we fib or withhold the truth to protect other people and not ourselves, we truly value relationships and take the high ground.
Relationships are complex and occasionally require small doses of dishonesty to safeguard others from harm or hurt.
